ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Inspection | Pittsburgh, PA
ut.description: Ultrasonic testing in Pittsburgh: thickness surveys on vessels, piping and tanks and UT weld inspection on mill and bridge steel. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection at Pittsburgh plants, mills, fabrication shops, gas facilities and river-side structures. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, take readings or examine welds to a written procedure, and hand back a report an Authorized Inspector, engineer or auditor can use. Send the component list through the Pittsburgh UT quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Pittsburgh

Pittsburgh is still a metals city. The Monongahela valley carries integrated steelmaking and coke-making, and the same river corridor holds rolling and finishing operations, forges, machine shops and heavy fabricators that grew up around the mills. Ultrasonic work follows that equipment. Maintenance groups ask for thickness surveys on pressure vessels, steam and condensate piping, process water lines and storage tanks, and for shear-wave examination of welds on crane runways, mill structures, lifting beams and repaired housings.

A second layer of demand came from the Appalachian gas build-out in western Pennsylvania. Compressor stations, gas processing plants, dehydration units, separators and the piping around them are carbon steel in wet service, so wall loss at low points, dead legs and injection points is the question owners need answered. Add the power plants and industrial boilers along the three rivers, the steel bridges that PennDOT and the counties maintain, and the shops that fabricate vessels, tanks and structural steel for all of them, and thickness and weld UT become routine work orders rather than special projects.

What UT finds and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing sends a sound pulse into steel and listens for the echo. On a thickness job the time between the front surface and back wall echo converts to remaining wall. On a weld job an angled beam travels through the weld volume and reflects from planar flaws such as lack of fusion, cracks and incomplete penetration, and from slag and porosity. That volumetric reach is the reason UT is chosen over surface methods when the question is what lies inside the weld or how much wall is left.

UT has limits that matter on Pittsburgh equipment. Heavy scale, pitting and rough external corrosion break up the coupling between probe and steel, so surfaces are cleaned or ground before measuring. Pitted wall can give a reading that looks acceptable beside a deep pit that the probe never crossed, which is why thickness grids and scanning around a point are used on corroded vessels. Coarse-grained castings and some thick weld metals scatter sound and reduce the usable range. Thin sections and very rough weld caps may need a different method or surface preparation first. UT does not replace a surface method for fine cracks open to the surface, and it will not tell you the material grade.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Pittsburgh UT work

The code depends on the item. Thickness measurement follows ASTM E797 and ASME Section V Article 23 (SE-797), with the readings feeding remaining-life and corrosion-rate calculations under API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for tanks. Weld examination follows ASME Section V Article 4 for the technique, while acceptance comes from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12, ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel, and AWS D1.5 for bridge work. Material examination of plate and forgings is covered by Article 5 and the product specification.

Pennsylvania adds its own layer. The state Department of Labor and Industry administers the boiler and unfired pressure vessel program, and vessels in its scope are inspected and certified under the state rules, which reference the National Board Inspection Code for repairs and alterations. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the owner-user inspection organization and its authorized inspector remain responsible for the inspection program. Atlantis performs the NDE and reports the data, such as thickness at condition monitoring locations, and the inspector of record decides what it means for fitness and next inspection date. OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), adds the mechanical integrity requirement at covered facilities.

How the examination is done

For thickness work the technician selects a dual-element probe for corroded or rough surfaces, calibrates the instrument on a step block of the same material at the same temperature range, and confirms against a known thickness before starting. Readings are taken at the established condition monitoring locations so each campaign is comparable with the last. The technician watches the A-scan rather than trusting a digital number alone, because doubling, lamination and pitting show up in the waveform before they show up in a bad reading. Hot lines need high-temperature probes, suitable couplant and a temperature correction; those settings are written into the procedure rather than improvised at the pipe.

For weld examination the surface is prepared, the weld is laid out, and an angle-beam probe, usually 45, 60 or 70 degrees, is calibrated on a block with a reference reflector. A reference level or distance-amplitude curve is built from side-drilled holes and the scan covers the weld and heat-affected zone from the faces the geometry allows. Indications are located along the weld and through the thickness, sized against the reference level, characterized and compared with the acceptance table named in the contract. Where geometry gives only one scanning face, the procedure says so, so the limitation travels with the result.

Typical Pittsburgh UT scopes at a glance

UT work by asset type around Pittsburgh
AssetUT taskReference
Process and gas facility vessels, separators, scrubbersThickness grids at shell, heads and nozzlesAPI 510, ASTM E797
Piping, dead legs, injection points and low pointsThickness at condition monitoring locationsAPI 570, ASME B31.3
Storage tank shells and roofsShell course thickness, repair verificationAPI 653
Crane runway girders, lifting beams, mill structuresShear-wave examination of groove weldsAWS D1.1, ASME Section V Article 4
Bridge steel on state and county spansWeld and plate examination per contractAWS D1.5
Boiler and steam piping at power and industrial plantsWall thickness and weld checks during outagesASME B31.1, ASME Section V

The scope is set by the damage mechanism the owner is worried about, not by a menu. Wet gas piping calls for low-point and dead-leg checks, steam condensate lines call for elbows and tees at flow changes, and a repaired crane girder calls for the repair weld and a margin of base metal on either side. Tell us which mechanism you are tracking and the crew plans around it.

Readings taken on a clean grid also show how the metal is wasting. A broad, even loss points to general corrosion. A scatter of low readings points to pitting, and a narrow band of loss along the bottom of a horizontal line points to water settling out of the process stream. Reporting the pattern, and not only the lowest number, helps the owner choose between monitoring, local repair and replacement.

When a surface cannot be prepared properly, the procedure should say so openly. A reading taken through thick paint or loose scale may be wrong by an unknown amount, so the report notes the surface condition at each location and flags any reading that does not meet the procedure.

Who does the work

')

Level II technicians set up and calibrate the equipment, perform the examination and interpret results. They are qualified by their employer under a written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedures and reviews the reports. Procedures are written to the governing code and edition for each job; if the contract names an older code edition, the procedure follows the contract. Atlantis has no office in Pittsburgh. Crews travel to your site with calibrated equipment, so mobilization is planned against your outage or shop schedule and confirmed when the quote is accepted.

What the UT report contains

  • Component or line identification, location and drawing or isometric reference
  • Procedure number and revision, and the code and edition applied
  • Instrument, probe, calibration block and couplant, with calibration checks recorded during the job
  • Technician name and qualification level
  • Thickness readings by grid or condition monitoring location, with the minimum highlighted, or weld indications with position, length, depth and amplitude
  • Accept or reject against the named acceptance table, plus sketches or thickness maps

Readings are laid out in the order your inspection program uses, so the next campaign can be compared line by line.

Planning a UT job in Pittsburgh

Pittsburgh work has local conditions that belong in the plan. Winters below freezing change couplant behavior and make bare steel hard to scan outdoors, so cold-weather couplant and sheltered work areas are agreed beforehand. Humid summers and river-valley fog cause condensation on cold pipe that interferes with coupling. Many mill, utility and gas sites require site-specific safety orientation, badging and permits before a technician can start, and scaffolding or rope access for elevated piping is usually the owner contractor. Hilly sites and tight valley access also affect where equipment can be staged. Turnarounds and mill outages set the calendar, so send your window early and share the line list so the crew size can be matched to the scope.

UT, MT or PT for your Pittsburgh job

Choose by the question. If you need remaining wall or a volumetric weld look, use UT. If the concern is surface or near-surface cracking in carbon steel, such as a crane hook or a weld toe, use magnetic particle testing in Pittsburgh. For stainless steel, aluminum or other non-magnetic material where cracks open to the surface are the worry, use liquid penetrant testing in Pittsburgh. Many jobs combine them: UT for wall and weld volume, then MT or PT on the repair area before it returns to service. Read the ultrasonic testing guide for method detail, and see our national UT service page. The Pennsylvania inspection hub lists the other services available across the state.

Training your own UT technicians in Pittsburgh

If your plant wants its own technicians, Atlantis offers UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, practice on the UT simulator, and a Pittsburgh NDT training page that explains the route. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own personnel, so a written practice is part of the picture; see written practice development if yours needs work.

faq.q: Do you perform ultrasonic thickness testing in Pittsburgh?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians are mobilized to your Pittsburgh site to measure wall thickness on vessels, piping and tanks at your condition monitoring locations, using a written procedure, calibrated equipment and the code you name. Atlantis has no office in the city, so the crew travels to the plant.

faq.q: Which code do you follow for UT weld inspection?
faq.a: The technique follows ASME Section V Article 4, and acceptance comes from the construction code for the item, such as ASME Section VIII, ASME B31.3, ASME B31.1, AWS D1.1 or AWS D1.5 for bridge steel. We confirm the code and edition before the job starts.

faq.q: Can UT be used instead of radiography on welds in Pittsburgh?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of welds, and ASME Section VIII allows it only under specific conditions. The substitution has to be agreed with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector before the work.

faq.q: Will your technicians take thickness readings on hot piping?
faq.a: Yes, where the procedure covers it. High-temperature probes, suitable couplant and a temperature correction are specified in advance, and safe access and surface temperature limits are confirmed with your site safety staff before anyone starts measuring.

faq.q: Who is responsible for the inspection under API 510, 570 or 653?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection program and its conclusions. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and reports the data, such as thickness at each condition monitoring location, so the inspector can calculate corrosion rate and remaining life.

faq.q: What surface condition do you need for UT?
faq.a: The surface must be clean enough for steady probe contact: loose scale, paint blisters and weld spatter removed, and weld caps dressed where the procedure requires it. Heavily pitted areas may need grinding or a scanned grid rather than single point readings.

faq.q: Does the Pennsylvania boiler and pressure vessel program affect my UT job?
faq.a: It can. Vessels and boilers in the state program are inspected under Pennsylvania rules that reference the National Board Inspection Code for repairs. We record procedure, technician and calibration data so the state or insurance inspector can review it.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for UT inspection in Pittsburgh?
faq.a: Send the component list, materials and wall thicknesses, the governing code, site location and your preferred dates through the quote request. We reply within one business day to confirm the scope, the procedure and how the crew will be mobilized.

faq.q: Can my own technicians learn UT through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis runs UT Level 1 and Level 2 training with a simulator and a route to certification under your written practice. Under SNT-TC-1A it is the employer that certifies the technician, after the required training and experience.

faq.q: What happens if the surface is too rough for a reliable UT reading?
faq.a: The procedure says the surface must be prepared first, and the report notes the surface condition at each location. A reading taken through heavy scale or paint is flagged as unreliable, and cleaning or grinding is requested before it is repeated.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Pittsburgh, PA | MT Testing
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Pittsburgh for welds, forgings, crane hooks and mill steel. On-site yoke and wet fluorescent MT to code. Get a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT provides on-site magnetic particle inspection (MPI) in Pittsburgh for welds, forgings, castings, crane hooks, mill components and structural steel. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, shop or job site, examine carbon and low-alloy steel for surface and near-surface cracks to a written procedure, and report each indication against the acceptance criteria you name. To scope a job, use the Pittsburgh MT quote request; we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Pittsburgh

Mag particle testing suits Pittsburgh because so much of the region is ferromagnetic steel under cyclic load. Around the Monongahela mills the candidates are roll necks and chocks, couplings and shafts, crane hooks, sheave blocks, ladle trunnions and the weld details on runway girders and mill buildings. Fatigue cracks in this equipment start at the surface, at a notch, a weld toe or a keyway, which is exactly what MT is built to find.

Away from the mills, the work shifts to fabrication and infrastructure. Fabricators in the metro area build pressure vessels, tanks, structural frames and equipment skids, and MT is the common surface check on fillet welds, attachment welds and repairs before paint or hydrotest. Steel bridges across the three rivers carry fatigue-sensitive details such as cover plate ends, stiffener welds and floor-beam connections, where inspection under AWS D1.5 or the owner contract often calls for MT on suspect welds. Gas compressor frames, piping support attachments and the power-plant headers along the rivers add further surface-crack scopes.

What MT finds and what it misses

MT works only on ferromagnetic material: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and most martensitic grades. A magnetic field is induced in the part; a crack or similar discontinuity across the field leaks flux, which holds fine iron particles in a visible line on the surface. It finds surface-breaking cracks, laps and seams, and cracks just under the surface, with sensitivity that drops quickly as the depth increases. Fine, tight fatigue cracks that other methods miss are often easy to see.

The limits are as important as the strengths. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper and nickel alloys cannot be examined this way, so those parts go to penetrant testing. A flaw lying parallel to the field lines produces little or no indication, which is why Article 7 requires two examinations at roughly right angles. Heavy paint, scale or weld spatter weakens the indication, and sharp geometry can produce non-relevant indications that a trained technician must tell apart from real cracks. MT shows where a crack is, not how deep it goes; depth sizing is a job for UT or grinding.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Pittsburgh MT work

The technique is governed by ASME Section V Article 7 for code work, and by ASTM E1444 for the practice and ASTM E709 for the guide. Acceptance depends on the item: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural welds, and AWS D1.5 for bridge welds, each with its own limits on linear and rounded indications. Forgings and castings use their product specifications, and lifting equipment follows the manufacturer and the applicable crane standard.

Pennsylvania boilers and unfired pressure vessels fall under the state Department of Labor and Industry program, and repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code, so MT after a weld repair is usually part of the record the inspector reviews. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the owner-user authorized inspector stays responsible for the inspection; Atlantis performs the MT and reports indications with location and size so the inspector can decide on repair or acceptance. Covered gas and process sites are also subject to OSHA process safety management, which expects mechanical-integrity inspection by recognized good engineering practice.

How the examination is done

For field work the usual tool is an AC electromagnetic yoke, chosen because it can be set between poles on the weld, moved quickly and used on structures. The Article 7 lifting-power check applies: an AC yoke must lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds. The technician confirms the yoke before use, cleans the surface, applies particles by dry powder or by a wet suspension in aerosol form, magnetizes in one direction, examines, then repeats at about ninety degrees. Prods can be used where a yoke does not reach, but arcing is a risk on finished surfaces, so the procedure says where prods are allowed.

Fluorescent wet particles give the highest sensitivity, and are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area with the intensity and ambient light limits the procedure states. Visible color-contrast particles over a thin white contrast paint suit well-lit field work. Field indicators or a pie-gage-type indicator confirm the field direction and strength in the part. After inspection, parts are demagnetized if residual fields would interfere with welding, machining, bearing performance or later operations, and the field is checked with a meter.

Reading and judging MT indications in Pittsburgh steel

A magnetic particle indication is only the start of the judgment. The technician classifies each one as relevant or non-relevant. A relevant indication is caused by a discontinuity such as a crack, lap or lack of fusion. A non-relevant one comes from a change in section, a keyway, a sharp thread root, a magnetic writing mark or the boundary of a heat-affected zone, and it can look like a crack until the surface is cleaned and re-examined. Pittsburgh work is full of these: old mill equipment has been repaired, welded, ground and re-machined many times, and each change leaves magnetic transitions that confuse a casual observer. Re-examination after light grinding, a change of magnetizing direction or a switch from dry powder to wet particles usually settles the question.

Relevant indications are then compared with the acceptance table. Linear indications are measured by length, rounded indications by diameter, and clusters by the number inside a defined area. Cracks are rejected under essentially every code. For a lifting device, any crack indication normally means the item is withdrawn until the owner and the manufacturer decide what happens next, so the report has to be exact about where the indication lies and how long it is.

Common MT scopes around Pittsburgh
ComponentTypical concernReference
Crane hooks, lifting beams, sheave blocksFatigue cracking at the throat or shankCrane standard and manufacturer
Runway girder and mill structure weldsToe cracks, repair weldsAWS D1.1
Bridge fatigue detailsStiffener and cover plate weldsAWS D1.5
Vessel and tank attachment weldsFillet and nozzle weld cracksASME Section VIII Appendix 6
Process and power piping weldsSurface cracking after repairASME B31.3, ASME B31.1

Surface preparation and coatings on Pittsburgh steel

Older Pittsburgh steel often carries decades of paint, mill scale and weld spatter. For magnetic particle work the surface needs to be free of loose scale, oil, grease and anything that would hold particles away from a crack or hide an indication. Thin, well-bonded coatings may be acceptable when the procedure has been demonstrated on a coated sample, but thick paint reduces the leakage field and can mask fine cracks, so it is removed locally at the weld or the area of concern. Blasting or wire brushing is the usual preparation; heavy grinding is avoided on fatigue-critical parts because it can create new surface damage. When a part is to be recoated afterward, the owner and the coating contractor should agree the cleanup so particles and contrast paint do not remain under the new film.

Who does the work

Level II technicians perform and interpret the examination. Qualification is by the employer under a written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews the reports. Procedures are written to the code and edition in your contract, not a generic template. Atlantis has no office in Pittsburgh; the crew travels to your site with yokes, particles, lights and meters, and the schedule is confirmed against your outage or shop window.

What the MT report contains

  • Part, weld or component identification and location
  • Procedure and revision, code and edition, and acceptance table applied
  • Method details: yoke or prod, current type, particle type and carrier, field direction checks, lighting readings for fluorescent work
  • Technician name and level
  • Each indication with location, orientation and length, accept or reject, and sketches or marked photos where useful
  • Demagnetization record when it was required

Planning an MT job in Pittsburgh

Pittsburgh weather affects magnetic particle work more than people expect. Cold steel in winter is slow to take a contrast paint, and some wet carriers become unusable near freezing, so the procedure should state the lowest working temperature or the part should be warmed. Summer humidity condenses on cold pipe and ruins particle mobility. Outdoor fluorescent inspection needs a tent or a shaded enclosure dark enough for the UV-A light, and day work on bridges or outdoor girders is often limited by sunlight. Mill and plant sites commonly need orientation, permits and escort, and elevated welds need access that the owner arranges. Send your outage dates and the weld count early so the crew can be sized.

MT, PT or UT for your Pittsburgh job

Use MT for surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, where it is fast and shows cracks plainly. Use dye penetrant inspection in Pittsburgh for stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic materials, or where particles cannot be applied. Use ultrasonic testing in Pittsburgh when you need weld volume examination or crack depth. The national MT service page, the MT guide and the MT versus PT comparison explain the trade-offs, and the Pennsylvania inspection hub lists related services.

Training your own MT technicians in Pittsburgh

Plants that want in-house capability can use MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, with the theory and practice that SNT-TC-1A expects. The Pittsburgh NDT training page describes how enrollment works, and practice tests help candidates prepare.

faq.q: Do you offer magnetic particle inspection in Pittsburgh?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians are mobilized to your Pittsburgh plant, fabrication shop or job site to examine welds, forgings, castings and structural steel with yokes, dry powder or wet particles, to a written procedure and the code named in your contract.

faq.q: What materials can MPI inspect?
faq.a: Magnetic particle inspection works on ferromagnetic materials only, such as carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic grades. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper and most nickel alloys are not magnetic, so those parts are examined by liquid penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: How deep can mag particle testing find cracks?
faq.a: MT finds cracks open to the surface and cracks lying just beneath it. Sensitivity falls off quickly with depth, so deeper flaws in welds are better examined by ultrasonic testing. MT also does not size crack depth.

faq.q: Why are two examination directions required?
faq.a: A crack lying parallel to the magnetic field gives almost no indication. ASME Section V Article 7 therefore calls for two examinations with the field at roughly right angles, so cracks running in any direction cross the flux and show up.

faq.q: Do you use fluorescent or visible particles on site?
faq.a: Both. Fluorescent wet particles are used where sensitivity is critical and the area can be darkened under UV-A light, while visible color-contrast particles suit well-lit outdoor work. The procedure states which applies, including the light levels required.

faq.q: Is demagnetization part of the job?
faq.a: When residual magnetism would affect welding, machining, bearings, instruments or later steps, the part is demagnetized and the field is checked with a meter. If no later step is affected, the procedure records that demagnetization was not required.

faq.q: Which acceptance criteria do you apply to MT indications?
faq.a: Acceptance comes from the construction code or contract, such as ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6, ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2, AWS D1.1 or AWS D1.5. The code and edition are confirmed in the quote and recorded on the report.

faq.q: Can MT be done on painted steel or in cold weather?
faq.a: Thin coatings can be examined if the procedure shows adequate sensitivity, and heavy coatings are removed locally. Cold affects carriers and contrast paint, so the lowest working temperature is stated in the procedure and the part is warmed if necessary.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for MT inspection in Pittsburgh?
faq.a: Send the component list, materials, number of welds or parts, governing code, location and preferred dates through the quote request. We reply within one business day to confirm scope and plan how the crew will be mobilized.

faq.q: Can MT be done on welds that have a coating or have been recently repaired?
faq.a: Thin, bonded coatings may be examined if the procedure has been demonstrated on a coated sample. Heavy coatings are removed locally. Repaired welds are examined after cooling, usually after the grind-out and weld, and again at the stage the code requires.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Penetrant | Pittsburgh, PA
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Pittsburgh on stainless, nickel alloy, aluminum and steel welds, castings and machined parts. Visible and fluorescent PT. Quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection, in Pittsburgh on stainless steel, nickel alloys, aluminum, titanium and carbon steel welds, castings and machined parts. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, follow a written PT procedure and report every indication against the acceptance criteria in your contract. Use the Pittsburgh PT quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Pittsburgh

Penetrant testing fills the gap that magnetic particle testing leaves. Pittsburgh has a long tradition of specialty metals work: stainless and nickel alloy fabrication, titanium and high-temperature alloy products, valves and pumps machined for the energy sector, and food and pharmaceutical process equipment built in stainless steel. None of these materials is magnetic, so surface cracks in them are found by penetrant. Typical PT subjects are pressure-part welds in stainless and alloy piping, weld repairs and grind-outs on carbon steel, machined sealing faces, castings and the finish of weld overlay.

The region also has power and process plants along the rivers, where PT is used on stainless feedwater and steam-chemistry piping, turbine hardware during outages and repair excavations that must be checked before welding resumes. At the gas facilities, PT is applied to valve bodies, stainless instrument tie-ins and non-ferrous fittings, and it is the usual choice for confirming that a crack has been fully removed before a repair weld is made.

What PT finds and what it misses

Liquid penetrant testing finds discontinuities open to the surface: cracks, laps, seams, porosity at the surface and lack of fusion that breaks the surface. The penetrant enters the opening by capillary action during the dwell time, the excess is removed, and a developer draws the liquid back out so it appears as a visible mark or fluorescent glow. The method works on any non-porous material, magnetic or not, which is its main advantage over MT.

PT is strictly a surface method. It will not find a flaw that is closed to the surface, buried in a weld or hidden under a smeared layer. Machining, grinding, blasting or peening can smear metal over a crack and seal its opening, so surfaces that have been worked must be etched or otherwise prepared before testing. Oil, paint, scale, rust and water in a defect keep penetrant out, so cleaning is a real part of the job and not a formality. Very rough or porous surfaces leave heavy background that can hide small indications.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Pittsburgh PT work

For code work the procedure follows ASME Section V Article 6, with ASTM E165 as the general-industry practice. Acceptance is taken from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, AWS D1.1 and D1.6 for structural and stainless weldments, and the product specification for castings. Pennsylvania boilers and unfired pressure vessels are covered by the state Department of Labor and Industry program, and PT on a repair weld forms part of the documentation the inspector reviews under the National Board Inspection Code.

Where API 510, 570 or 653 governs, the owner-user authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection and the decision on a defect. Atlantis performs the PT and reports indication locations and sizes. Covered facilities also work under OSHA process safety management, whose mechanical-integrity element expects inspection by recognized good engineering practice.

How the examination is done

The technician first confirms the penetrant materials, the procedure and the part temperature. Article 6 sets a standard range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials; outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature. The surface is cleaned, usually with solvent and wipes in the field, and dried completely. Penetrant is applied by spray or brush and left for the dwell time in the procedure. Excess is removed by solvent wipe, water or an emulsifier depending on the system, taking care not to wash penetrant out of fine cracks. Developer is applied thinly and evenly, the development time is observed, and the surface is examined in adequate white light for visible dye or in a darkened area under UV-A light for fluorescent penetrant.

Visible red dye is the usual field choice because it needs no darkened enclosure. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive and is chosen when the code, part class or crack size demands. After inspection, residues are removed so that they do not affect welding, coating or service, which matters especially on stainless steel and nickel alloys where chloride and sulfur contamination from some materials must be controlled.

Controlling the penetrant process in Pittsburgh field work

Good penetrant testing is mostly process discipline. The cleaning step removes oil, grease, paint and corrosion product; the dry step makes sure solvent or water has left the crack; the dwell is long enough for the penetrant to enter fine cracks; the removal step takes off the surface film without pulling penetrant out of the defect; and the developer is applied thin and even. A technician who skips any of these steps can miss a real crack or create false indications, so the procedure lists each step with its time or condition and the report records what was done.

Interpretation also takes judgment. A true crack tends to show as a continuous or intermittent sharp line that bleeds out slowly, while porosity shows as round dots and a scratch or machining mark shows as a short irregular line that disappears when wiped and re-developed. Light bleed-out around a rough weld toe can look like a defect when it is only residual penetrant, and heavy background after poor removal can hide small flaws. When an indication is doubtful, the technician wipes it, waits, re-applies developer and observes again, and it is classified and measured against the code table.

Surface preparation, contamination and stainless steel in Pittsburgh

Penetrant testing depends on a surface that lets liquid reach the crack. Pittsburgh fabrication and plant work brings several problems: paint and scale on older equipment, oil and cutting fluid on machined parts, welding flux and spatter on new welds, and smeared metal from grinding or wire brushing. Each has its own cure: solvent cleaning for oil and grease, mechanical removal for scale and flux, and light etching where metal has been smeared over the opening of a flaw. Wire brushes used on stainless steel must be stainless and dedicated to that purpose, because carbon steel particles embedded in the surface cause corrosion later and can also produce false indications.

Penetrant materials for stainless steel and nickel alloys are normally purchased with low halogen and sulfur content, and the lot analysis is kept with the job record. This matters on piping that will operate at temperature or in chloride-bearing service, and it is why the report lists lot numbers. After testing, all penetrant and developer is removed by solvent wipe so that the surface is clean for welding, coating or service. Wipes and rags are disposed of under the site rules, since many Pittsburgh facilities restrict solvents and aerosol cans inside process areas or require a hot-work permit before use.

Who does the work

Level II technicians apply the penetrant system and interpret the result. They are qualified by the employer under a written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Atlantis has no office in Pittsburgh. Crews travel to your site with their own materials, lights and test panels, and the schedule is agreed when the quote is accepted.

What the PT report contains

  • Component or weld identification, material and surface condition
  • Procedure and revision, code and edition, and acceptance criteria
  • Penetrant type, removal method, developer form, lot numbers, dwell and development times, and part temperature
  • Light conditions, and UV-A readings for fluorescent work
  • Technician name and level
  • Indications with location, size and type, accept or reject, and photos or sketches

Planning a PT job in Pittsburgh

Temperature and moisture decide most Pittsburgh PT planning. A river-valley winter pushes steel under the 40 degree lower limit, so the part has to be warmed and held in range or the procedure qualified at the lower temperature. Humid summer days condense water on cold pipe and make drying slow, and water left in a defect will block the penetrant. Outdoor work in rain or wind needs shelter. Sites often require orientation, permits and hot-work coordination, and stainless surfaces may need contamination-controlled consumables, which must be named in the quote. Send us the outage window, the alloys and the number of welds early.

PT, MT or UT for your Pittsburgh job

Choose PT for non-magnetic alloys and for surface cracks where the part cannot be magnetized. Choose magnetic particle testing in Pittsburgh for carbon and low-alloy steel, where it is faster and also catches near-surface flaws. Choose ultrasonic testing in Pittsburgh for wall thickness and weld volume. See the national PT service page, the MT versus PT comparison and the Pennsylvania inspection hub.

Training your own PT technicians in Pittsburgh

For in-house capability, Atlantis offers PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, plus the PT simulator for practice. The Pittsburgh NDT training page explains local enrollment, and the Article 6 explainer covers the code requirements.

faq.q: Do you provide liquid penetrant testing in Pittsburgh?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians are mobilized to your Pittsburgh site to carry out dye penetrant inspection on welds, castings and machined parts, using a written procedure and the acceptance criteria in your contract. Atlantis has no office in the city.

faq.q: What defects can dye penetrant inspection find?
faq.a: PT finds discontinuities open to the surface, such as cracks, laps, seams and surface porosity. It does not find flaws that are closed or buried below the surface, which is why smeared or machined surfaces need preparation before testing.

faq.q: Which materials can PT be used on?
faq.a: Penetrant testing works on any non-porous material, including stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, nickel alloys and carbon steel. It is the normal choice for non-magnetic alloys that magnetic particle testing cannot examine.

faq.q: What temperature limits apply to field PT?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 sets a standard range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the penetrant materials. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature, which matters in a Pittsburgh winter.

faq.q: Should I choose visible or fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible red dye works in ordinary light and suits most field jobs. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive but needs a darkened area and UV-A light. The code, the part class and the expected crack size decide which one is specified.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be used on welds that have been ground?
faq.a: Yes, but grinding and machining can smear metal over a crack and close its opening. The surface is etched or otherwise prepared per the procedure so that the penetrant can enter any surface-breaking flaw.

faq.q: Is the PT report suitable for state or insurance review?
faq.a: The report records procedure, code, materials, lot numbers, times, temperature, technician and results, so an Authorized Inspector, a Pennsylvania boiler and pressure vessel inspector or an auditor can follow exactly what was done.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for PT inspection in Pittsburgh?
faq.a: Send the components, alloys, number of welds or parts, governing code, site and dates through the quote request. We reply within one business day to confirm the scope and the way the crew will be mobilized to your site.

faq.q: Why do you record penetrant lot numbers on the report?
faq.a: Lot numbers tie the result to the exact penetrant, cleaner and developer used. On stainless steel and nickel alloys they also let the owner check halogen and sulfur content, and they let an auditor trace the materials if a question comes up later.

faq.q: Do you test the repair excavation before welding resumes?
faq.a: Yes, when the scope calls for it. After a crack is ground out, the excavation is tested to prove the flaw is gone, and the finished repair weld is tested again. Both results go into the report so the repair history is complete.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing in Pittsburgh, PA | UT & Level III
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. In Pittsburgh we offer UT as a volumetric alternative, Level III review of radiographs and RT theory.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania: What Atlantis Offers
rt.html:
If you searched for radiographic testing in Pittsburgh, here is the plain answer: Atlantis NDT does not perform radiographic testing in the United States. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity, regulated under the Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules in 10 CFR Part 34 or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and it is not a service Atlantis offers here. What Atlantis does offer is a set of options that often answer the same question without a radiation source.

Ultrasonic testing as the volumetric alternative in Pittsburgh

When the real need is to know what is inside a weld, ultrasonic examination can be a volumetric alternative where the construction code and the owner allow it. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 has its own acceptance criteria for ultrasonic examination of groove welds, and ASME Section VIII permits ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only under specific conditions. None of these is automatic. The substitution is agreed with the owner, the design engineer and, on code work, the authorized inspector before the job begins, and the procedure is written to the code that governs the weld.

Atlantis technicians are mobilized to Pittsburgh sites for this work; there is no office in the city. See ultrasonic testing in Pittsburgh for the weld and thickness service, and send the weld details if you want an opinion on whether UT fits your code.

ASNT Level III radiography services that need no radiation licence

Reviewing radiographic evidence does not require a source license, because no exposure is made. Atlantis can review radiographs, whether film or digital images, together with the technique sheets that produced them, against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. A second read on a disputed indication is a common request in Pittsburgh fabrication, where a shop and an owner sometimes disagree about whether a mark is slag, porosity or a crack. Atlantis can also review an RT contractor's procedure and written practice for completeness and code compliance before work starts.

  • Independent interpretation of radiographs and digital images against the code acceptance criteria
  • Review of technique sheets, sensitivity, density and image quality indicators
  • Second opinion on disputed or borderline indications
  • Review of an RT contractor's procedure, personnel qualification records and written practice

This work is led by ASNT NDT Level III personnel, including our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis does not recommend or name radiography contractors, since the owner chooses and contracts the licensed company directly.

Pittsburgh jobs where this comes up

Radiography questions in Pittsburgh usually arise on pressure vessel and piping fabrication, structural and crane weld repair in the Monongahela mills, pipeline and compressor station welds in the gas build-out, and power plant piping. In each case the owner holds the code and the acceptance decision. Pennsylvania pressure vessels and boilers are covered by the Department of Labor and Industry program, which references the National Board Inspection Code, so documentation quality matters. A second reviewer with Level III authority can catch an interpretation problem before it becomes a rejected data book.

Training in radiography theory

If you want your own staff to understand radiographic interpretation, Atlantis teaches a theory course: RT Level 2 course. It covers principles, image quality and interpretation under the SNT-TC-1A recommended practice. It does not replace radiation safety training or a state or federal radiographer license, which are separate requirements. See the Pittsburgh NDT training page for enrollment.

Other Atlantis inspection in Pittsburgh

For surface cracks and wall loss the options are magnetic particle testing, liquid penetrant testing and ultrasonic thickness testing, all performed by technicians mobilized to your site. The Pennsylvania inspection hub lists the full range, and Level III consulting covers procedures and report review.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in Pittsburgh?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under NRC rules or Agreement State rules. Instead, Atlantis supplies ultrasonic testing, Level III review of radiographs, and RT theory training.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my Pittsburgh weld?
faq.a: Sometimes, where the construction code and owner allow it. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 have ultrasonic provisions, and ASME Section VIII allows it only under specific conditions. The owner, the design engineer and the authorized inspector have to sign off on any switch before the work is scoped.

faq.q: Can you review radiographs taken by another company?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and the technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, and give a second read on any disputed indication. No radiation source is involved.

faq.q: Can you review an RT contractor's procedure or written practice?
faq.a: Yes. A Level III review checks the procedure against the code, the technique sheet content, image quality indicators and the written practice for personnel qualification, so gaps are found before the contractor starts work.

faq.q: Do you teach radiographic testing?
faq.a: Atlantis teaches a Level 2 theory course for RT under SNT-TC-1A. It does not replace radiation safety training or a radiographer license, which are separate legal requirements handled by the licensed radiography employer.
